# FNT02 oracle fixtures

## `oracle.txt`

Expected glyph outlines for every glyph in four fonts — **4,161 glyphs**,
2,111 of them composite.

Every number in it was produced by **fontTools**, reading the font files named
in the `FONT` lines. This crate never contributed a value to it.

### Why an independent implementation

Reading an outline is transcription, and the format goes out of its way to make
transcription hard:

- `loca` offsets come in two formats, and the short one stores *half* the real
  offset. Reading one as the other does not fail — it lands inside `glyf` and
  decodes into a glyph-shaped thing that is not the glyph.
- The flag array is run-length encoded, so one wrong repeat count shifts every
  point after it.
- Each coordinate's *width in bytes* is carried by flag bits, and one of those
  bits means "positive" in one combination and "occupies no bytes at all" in
  another. Guess wrong and every later read is misaligned.

A fixture hand-written alongside the parser shares its author's understanding
of all three, so both are wrong together and agree perfectly. This repository
has now hit that shape five times — a zstd encoder agreeing with its own
decoder, Anki fixtures generated by the code they tested, an emitted Vite
project asserted as text and never built, a PDF writer whose `FlateDecode` was
raw deflate, and a deck layout that looked right on the web while stripping
colour from Flutter.

### Two levels

- `D` lines: one FNV-1a digest per glyph, for **every** glyph. This is the
  coverage — no glyph goes unchecked — at the cost of only saying *which* glyph
  broke.
- `G` lines: a sampled ~40 glyphs per font recorded point by point, so a
  failure says *what* differs. The test compares these first, because a full
  diff is more useful than a pair of hashes.

FNV-1a rather than SHA-256 so both sides compute it in five lines with no
dependency. This guards against mistakes, not adversaries.

### Regenerating

```bash
python3 code/scripts/generate_glyph_oracle.py
```

Requires `fonttools`. Rerun only when adding a font or changing the sampling —
a diff in `oracle.txt` at any other time means decoded outlines changed, which
is exactly the thing this file exists to notice.

## The fonts

| Font | Licence | Why it is here |
|---|---|---|
| `Inter-Regular.ttf` | SIL OFL 1.1 | Long `loca`; 1,881 composite glyphs |
| `NotoSansTamil-Static.ttf` | SIL OFL 1.1 | Short `loca`; a script Engram ships decks for |
| `NotoSansJP-Subset.ttf` | SIL OFL 1.1 | Short `loca`; CJK, the case that forces subsetting |

All three already lived in the repository; none was added for this crate.

## `synthetic.ttf`

Built by `generate_glyph_oracle.py` using fontTools' `FontBuilder`.

It exists because of a gap found by looking: across Inter and thirteen Noto
faces — every font in this repository — **not one composite glyph uses a scale,
a 2×2 transform, nesting, or anchor-point placement.** They are all plain
translations. Those branches of the parser would otherwise have been written,
shipped, and never once executed.

This font contains one glyph for each: uniform scale, x/y scale, a 30° rotation
(not axis-aligned, so a transposed matrix gives different numbers rather than
the same ones), a composite whose component is itself a composite, anchor-point
placement, and a 0.5 scale over odd negative coordinates — that last one to pin
the rounding rule, since round-half-up and round-half-away-from-zero agree on
+37.5 and disagree on −37.5.

fontTools writes the font and reads back the **saved bytes** to produce the
expectations, so this is still a cross-implementation check rather than a
fixture agreeing with itself. Reading back the saved file rather than the
in-memory objects matters: the compiled bytes are what the parser sees.
